one_liner: CUDA framework whose fully fused small-MLP kernels train and infer 2x-10x faster than TensorFlow 2.5 XLA (RTX 3090).
what_it_does: A self-contained C++/CUDA library for training and querying small neural networks on NVIDIA GPUs, best known for the fully fused MLP and the multiresolution hash-grid encoding behind Instant NGP. Models are built from a JSON config (encoding, network, loss, optimizer) with tcnn::create_from_config, then trained with trainer->training_step on GPUMatrix batches and queried with network->inference. A PyTorch extension (tinycudann) exposes the same modules as torch.nn layers. It is its own framework, not a drop-in for TensorFlow or cuDNN.
how_it_is_fast: The fully fused MLP evaluates every layer of a narrow network in one kernel: each thread block keeps its slice of the batch's activations in shared memory, loads weight tiles into registers and runs the matrix products on tensor cores via WMMA 16x16x16 FP16 fragments, so intermediate activations never go to global memory and there is one launch per pass instead of one per layer. Hidden widths are template parameters (16/32/64/128) and shared-memory rows are skewed by 8 halfs to avoid bank conflicts. Version 2.0 adds JIT fusion: the model is emitted as a CUDA device function and compiled with NVRTC, optionally fused with the caller's own kernel (Instant NGP fuses its whole NeRF ray marcher this way).
when_to_use: Neural fields, NeRF/neural radiance caching, SDFs and other coordinate networks: millions of points per step through MLPs 16-128 neurons wide, often after a hash-grid or frequency encoding.
Online training inside a renderer or simulator where both training and inference must run every frame on the GPU.
Large batches (2^14 and up); the README says PyTorch-binding overhead roughly doubles runtime at 64k batch but is much smaller from 256k.
Tensor-core NVIDIA GPUs (compute capability above 7.0, e.g. Turing and newer) with enough shared memory; the README names RTX 2080 Ti / RTX 3090 or higher for the default fully fused configuration.
when_not_to_use: Wide or general networks: FullyFusedMLP accepts only 16, 32, 64 or 128 neurons per hidden layer; anything else needs the slower CutlassMLP, and convolutions, attention or recurrent layers are not provided.
Non-NVIDIA hardware, CPUs, or GPUs at or below compute capability 7.0: the fully fused path is not compiled there and falls back to CutlassMLP; FP32 builds also fall back.
Lower-end or some data-center GPUs where the default shared-memory footprint does not fit (issue #511 reports the insufficient-shared-memory error on an A100 at 64 neurons, open with no reply).
Teams without CUDA build expertise: about 240 open issues, dominated by pip/CMake/Windows/new-GPU build failures; there are no tagged releases after 2.0.
Small batches or per-sample latency work: batch sizes must be multiples of 256 (BATCH_SIZE_GRANULARITY) and the kernels are tuned for throughput.

integration.form: static lib (CMake add_subdirectory; builds the tiny-cuda-nn STATIC target) or PyTorch extension via pip from bindings/torch
integration.dependencies: CUDA toolkit; NVRTC for JIT fusion (TCNN_BUILD_WITH_RTC, on by default); bundled submodules CUTLASS, fmt and nlohmann/json; cuBLAS/cuSolver only for the Shampoo optimizer (off by default); PyTorch for the bindings
integration.min_toolchain: C++17, CMake 3.21+ per README (CMakeLists says 3.18), GCC 8+ or Visual Studio 2019/2022, CUDA 10.2+ on Linux or 11.5+ on Windows
integration.platforms: Linux and Windows with an NVIDIA GPU; fully fused MLP needs compute capability > 7.0 and FP16 (TCNN_HALF_PRECISION, default on except sm_61 and <= sm_52); targets up to sm_120 with recent CUDA
integration.thread_safety: not documented; work is issued on caller-supplied CUDA streams and models hold mutable training state, so treat each model as single-owner

gotchas: The fully fused forward and backward passes throw unless network precision is __half, so outputs and gradients are FP16; mixed-precision accuracy is your problem to check.
Unsupported widths, too-old GPUs or FP32 builds silently degrade to CutlassMLP (a log warning), which is much slower; check the logged network type.
JIT fusion is opt-in (set_jit_fusion) and the README warns it can slow training for hash grids over ~20M parameters, MLPs wider than 128, or RTX 3000-series and older GPUs; measure both modes.
The README benchmark caption still names benchmarks/bench_ours.cu and bench_tensorflow.py, which moved to benchmarks/image/.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick tiny-cuda-nn over ThunderKittens or FlashAttention-3 when the workload is many tiny MLP evaluations (neural fields) rather than large GEMMs or attention, and over RTNeural when you have an NVIDIA GPU and huge batches instead of per-sample CPU inference; for CPU small-GEMM building blocks LIBXSMM is the closer fit.
verified_claims_summary: The only external comparison is the author's chart: fully fused MLPs 64 and 128 neurons wide vs TensorFlow 2.5.0 with XLA (whose script also runs the matmuls in FP16) on an RTX 3090, learning an image at batch sizes 2^14-2^21; read approximately, 64-wide training is about 10x faster at 2^14 narrowing to about 2x at 2^21, and inference about 8x at 2^21. CUDA, driver and compiler versions are not stated; the 1.5x-2.5x JIT-fusion and 5x Instant NGP figures are against tiny-cuda-nn's own earlier path, not an external baseline.
status_note: Active (last commit 2026-09-29, 4.5k stars, used by Instant NGP, Nerfstudio and NerfAcc) and BSD-3-Clause per LICENSE.txt, so copyable, but builds are fragile and the last tagged release is 2.0.
